lapita-erreicht-tonga-und-samoa#title: Lapita settlers reach Tonga and Samoa
lapita-erreicht-tonga-und-samoa#summary: With Fiji, Tonga and Samoa the Lapita seafarers reach the western edge of Polynesia, where Polynesian culture takes shape over the following centuries.
lapita-erreicht-tonga-und-samoa#text: After leaving the Bismarck Archipelago, the bearers of the Lapita culture pushed further east via the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia. Between about 1000 and 800 BC they reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa; the oldest settlement traces in Tonga are among the earliest evidence in Polynesia. A long pause of well over a thousand years followed, during which the language, beliefs and society of the Polynesians developed in Tonga and Samoa. Pottery later fell out of use in West Polynesia, so the islands further east were settled without ceramics.
funan-und-oc-eo#title: Funan and the Port of Óc Eo
funan-und-oc-eo#summary: In the Mekong Delta Funan emerges as the first known major state of Southeast Asia, its port of Óc Eo linking trade routes between India and China.
funan-und-oc-eo#text: What we know about Funan comes mainly from Chinese sources; the name is Chinese and may render a local word for "mountain". Chinese envoys who visited the country around the middle of the 3rd century reported walled cities, taxes paid in gold and pearls, and an Indian script. According to a legend, a Brahmin named Kaundinya married a local female ruler and so founded the dynasty. Excavations at Óc Eo in what is now southern Vietnam have uncovered jewellery from India, mirrors from China and Roman coins of the 2nd century. In the 6th and 7th centuries Funan was absorbed into the Khmer kingdom of Chenla.
gruendung-von-champa#summary: On the coast of present-day central Vietnam the kingdom of the Cham emerges, which will survive for more than a thousand years between the Khmer Empire and Vietnam.
gruendung-von-champa#text: Chinese chronicles report that around 192 a local leader in the south of the Chinese commandery of Rinan broke away; this gave rise to the kingdom of Linyi, regarded as the forerunner of Champa. The Cham spoke an Austronesian language, were skilled seafarers and lived from trade in agarwood, ivory and other goods. Their rulers adopted Hinduism and Sanskrit and built numerous temples to Shiva at Mỹ Sơn. Champa consisted of several principalities that fought wars alternately with Angkor and Đại Việt; in 1177 the Cham even sacked Angkor. After the fall of its capital Vijaya in 1471 Champa shrank, and in 1832 Vietnam annexed the last remnant.
gruendung-konstantinopels#summary: On the site of the Greek city of Byzantium, a new capital of the Roman Empire rises on the Bosporus.
gruendung-konstantinopels#text: From 324 Constantine the Great had old Byzantium lavishly rebuilt, and on 11 May 330 he dedicated it as his new residence. The city received palaces, churches, a forum and a great Hippodrome, and later became a second Rome with its own senate. Its position on the strait between Europe and Asia, at the junction of trade routes and close to the threatened frontiers on the Danube and Euphrates, gave it strategic and economic importance. As Constantinople it remained the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for more than eleven centuries.
bau-der-theodosianischen-mauern#summary: Under Emperor Theodosius II, Constantinople receives a land wall that protects the city for more than a thousand years.
bau-der-theodosianischen-mauern#text: Around 413 a new land wall was completed west of the old city limits, greatly enlarging the urban area. After an earthquake in 447 it was quickly repaired and expanded into a layered system of moat, outer wall and main wall with numerous towers. Avars, Arabs, Bulgarians and Rus all failed before the walls. Only the crusaders in 1204, who attacked from the sea side, and the Ottomans in 1453 with their great cannon took the city.
konzil-von-chalkedon#summary: An imperial council declares that Christ exists in two natures, as true God and true man.
konzil-von-chalkedon#text: Emperor Marcian summoned the council to Chalcedon, across the water from Constantinople, to settle a bitter dispute over the nature of Christ. The bishops decided that Christ is both God and man in two natures, without confusion and without division. In addition, the bishop of Constantinople was given second rank after Rome. Many Christians in Egypt, Syria and Armenia rejected the decisions; this split gave rise to churches such as the Coptic and the Syriac Orthodox, and the dispute strained relations between these provinces and the capital.
corpus-iuris-civilis#summary: A commission under Tribonian gathers the whole of Roman law into a single code, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis.
corpus-iuris-civilis#text: In 529 a first collection of imperial laws, the Codex, appeared; in 533 it was followed by the Digest, with excerpts from the writings of Roman jurists, and the Institutes, a textbook for legal teaching, and in 534 by a revised edition of the Codex. Justinian's new laws, the Novels, were added later. The work received the name Corpus Juris Civilis only in the 16th century. From the 11th century it was rediscovered and taught in Bologna and so became the basis of civil law in large parts of Europe.
nika-aufstand#summary: An uprising in the Hippodrome brings Justinian to the brink of overthrow and ends in a bloodbath.
nika-aufstand#text: In January 532 the circus factions of the Blues and the Greens, usually bitter rivals, joined forces against the emperor and his hated ministers; their battle cry "Nika!", "Conquer!", gave the uprising its name. The rioters set large parts of the city on fire, including the old Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed a rival emperor. According to Procopius, Justinian wanted to flee, but Theodora persuaded him to stay. Troops under Belisarius and Mundus trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome; according to the sources, some 30,000 people were killed.
vandalenkrieg-belisars#summary: A small Byzantine army conquers the kingdom of the Vandals in North Africa in a short campaign.
vandalenkrieg-belisars#text: In 533 Justinian sent his general Belisarius with a fleet to North Africa, where the Vandals had ruled their own kingdom from Carthage since 439. After victories at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum Belisarius entered Carthage, and King Gelimer surrendered in 534. Belisarius celebrated a triumph in Constantinople such as had not been seen for centuries. North Africa remained Byzantine until the Arab capture of Carthage in 698, but was often unsettled by Berber revolts.
gotenkrieg#title: War against the Ostrogoths in Italy
gotenkrieg#summary: In a war lasting almost twenty years Byzantium wins Italy back from the Ostrogoths, but devastates the country in the process.
gotenkrieg#text: In 535 Belisarius began the reconquest of Italy, occupied Sicily, Naples and Rome, and in 540 took the Gothic capital of Ravenna. Under King Totila, however, the Ostrogoths regained large parts of Italy. Only the general Narses defeated them in 552 at the battle of Busta Gallorum, in which Totila fell, and broke their resistance by 554. After the long war Italy was impoverished and depopulated, and as early as 568 the Lombards conquered much of the country; Ravenna remained the seat of Byzantine administration until 751.
justinianische-pest#summary: The first known plague pandemic reaches the Mediterranean via Egypt and claims countless victims in Constantinople in 542.
justinianische-pest#text: The disease appeared in 541 at Pelusium in Egypt and reached Constantinople in the spring of 542, where, according to Procopius, thousands of people died each day at its height; Justinian himself fell ill but survived. Over the following two centuries the disease returned again and again. DNA analyses of skeletons have confirmed that the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis was the cause. How many people died in total, and how badly the plague weakened the empire's economy and military power, are debated among historians.
schmuggel-der-seidenraupen#summary: According to Procopius, monks smuggle silkworm eggs from Central Asia into the empire.
schmuggel-der-seidenraupen#text: For a long time silk had to be imported at great expense through Persia, which controlled the trade. Procopius reports that around 552 monks who had lived in a land called Serinda offered Justinian to obtain silkworm eggs and brought them to Constantinople hidden in hollow canes. Where Serinda lay is unclear; Central Asia is the usual suggestion. From then on the empire developed its own silk production, which was under state supervision and supplied precious fabrics for the court, the church and diplomacy.
sieg-des-herakleios-ueber-die-perser#sum: After a quarter of a century of war, Emperor Heraclius defeats the Sasanians near Nineveh and forces a peace.
sieg-des-herakleios-ueber-die-perser#tex: Since 602 the Persians under Khosrow II had conquered Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt, carried off the True Cross from Jerusalem in 614 and besieged Constantinople together with the Avars in 626. Heraclius dared a campaign deep into Persian territory and defeated the Persian army near Nineveh in December 627. Khosrow was overthrown in 628, and the Persians returned all conquered territories and the Cross, which Heraclius solemnly brought back to Jerusalem in 630. Both empires, however, were so exhausted that they could offer little resistance to the Arab attacks that soon followed.
schlacht-am-jarmuk#summary: An Arab Muslim army defeats the Byzantines on the Yarmuk river; Syria and Palestine are lost.
schlacht-am-jarmuk#text: In August 636, on the Yarmuk, a tributary of the Jordan, the armies of Caliph Umar met a large Byzantine force that Heraclius had assembled. After several days of fighting the Byzantine army was crushed. Heraclius gave up Syria, Jerusalem fell in 638, and between 640 and 642 the Arabs also conquered Egypt, Constantinople's granary. The empire thus lost its richest provinces and became a smaller state that relied on Asia Minor, the Balkans and parts of Italy.
einsatz-des-griechischen-feuers#summary: Byzantium deploys a new incendiary weapon that keeps burning even on water and drives back Arab fleets.
einsatz-des-griechischen-feuers#text: According to the chronicler Theophanes, around 672 an architect named Kallinikos, a refugee from Syria, brought the recipe to Constantinople. The liquid was sprayed from tubes onto enemy ships, ignited and could hardly be put out with water. It helped to repel the Arab attacks on Constantinople in the 670s and in 717/718. Its composition was a state secret and is still not known for certain; it probably contained petroleum. The exact dating of the first Arab siege is also disputed.
aufstieg-von-srivijaya#summary: An inscription near Palembang on Sumatra records the military expedition of a ruler who makes Srivijaya the leading power on the Strait of Malacca.
aufstieg-von-srivijaya#text: The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 682 is written in Old Malay and describes a successful campaign with which Srivijaya established its power. From Palembang the kingdom soon controlled the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, through which maritime trade between India and China passed. The Chinese monk Yijing, who stayed there in 671 and again later, reported more than a thousand Buddhist monks and advised pilgrims to learn Sanskrit in Srivijaya. Srivijaya was probably more a league of ports under a leading city than a unified state. After an attack by the south Indian Chola Empire in 1025 it lost importance and broke up in the 13th century.
beginn-des-bilderstreits#summary: Emperor Leo III turns against the veneration of religious images and sets off a dispute lasting decades.
beginn-des-bilderstreits#text: According to the later, pro-image tradition, Leo III had an image of Christ removed from the palace gate in 726 and banned the veneration of images in 730; how far he actually went is disputed among historians. The opponents of images, the iconoclasts, regarded the veneration of icons as idolatry, while their supporters, the iconophiles, defended it as a path to the holy. Leo's son Constantine V had hostility to images declared church doctrine at a council in 754 and persecuted image-venerating monks. The dispute divided church and society and also estranged Byzantium from the pope in Rome.
zweites-konzil-von-nicaea#summary: At the instigation of Empress Irene, a council permits the veneration of images once again.
zweites-konzil-von-nicaea#text: Irene was ruling for her underage son Constantine VI and in 787 convened a council at Nicaea, which papal envoys also attended. The bishops decided that images of Christ, Mary and the saints may be venerated but not worshipped; the veneration is directed at the person depicted, not at the image. It was the last council recognized as ecumenical by both the Orthodox and the Catholic churches. In 815, however, the emperors returned to iconoclasm.
borobudur-und-prambanan#summary: In Central Java the Buddhist monument of Borobudur and the Hindu temples of Prambanan rise as two of the largest religious buildings in Asia.
borobudur-und-prambanan#text: Borobudur was built roughly between 780 and 830 under the Buddhist Shailendra dynasty. The vast stepped structure encases a hill; pilgrims circle through nine levels past more than 2,600 reliefs that tell of the life of the Buddha and the path to enlightenment, until they reach the round terraces with 72 perforated stupas. Only a few kilometres away, rulers of the Mataram dynasty built Prambanan, which according to an inscription was consecrated in 856; the tallest temple is dedicated to Shiva, and reliefs tell the Ramayana. After the centre of Javanese power moved east in the 10th century, both complexes fell into decay. Borobudur was uncovered again in 1814 under British administration and restored with UNESCO help between 1973 and 1983.
jayavarman-ii-begruendet-khmer-reich#tit: Jayavarman II Founds the Khmer Empire
jayavarman-ii-begruendet-khmer-reich#sum: On Mount Kulen Jayavarman II is consecrated as universal monarch, laying the foundation of the Khmer Empire of Angkor.
jayavarman-ii-begruendet-khmer-reich#tex: According to an 11th-century inscription, Jayavarman II returned from "Java" (whether this means the island or another kingdom is disputed) and united the Khmer principalities in decades of fighting. In 802 he was consecrated as chakravartin, universal monarch, in a ceremony on Phnom Kulen northeast of the later Angkor, and declared the land independent. This was linked to a cult of the god-king, the devaraja, whose exact meaning is debated by scholars. His successors moved the capital to the plain north of the Tonle Sap lake, where Yasodharapura, the later Angkor, arose around 900. The Khmer Empire dominated large parts of mainland Southeast Asia until the 13th century.
goettrik-zerstoert-reric#title: King Godfred Destroys Reric and Strengthens the Danevirke
goettrik-zerstoert-reric#summary: The Danish king Godfred destroys the Slavic trading place of Reric, moves its merchants into his realm and has the border rampart against the Frankish Empire extended.
goettrik-zerstoert-reric#text: The Royal Frankish Annals report that in 808 Godfred destroyed the Baltic trading place of Reric, in the territory of the Obodrites, who were allied with Charlemagne, and brought its merchants into his own kingdom, probably to Hedeby on the Schlei. At the same time he had the border with the Franks secured by a rampart that is considered part of the Danevirke. Over the following two centuries Hedeby became one of the most important trading places in northern Europe. Godfred’s actions show that there were already kings in Denmark around 800 who deliberately controlled trade and borders.
ansgar-missioniert-in-birka#summary: Around 830 the Frankish monk Ansgar preaches in the Swedish trading town of Birka, one of the earliest Christian missions in Scandinavia.
ansgar-missioniert-in-birka#text: Ansgar, a monk of Corvey, travelled around 829/830 with an embassy of Louis the Pious to Birka on Lake Mälaren, where the king allowed him to preach. Some inhabitants were baptized, but no lasting church was established. In 831 Ansgar became archbishop of the newly founded see of Hamburg, which Vikings destroyed in 845; afterwards he led the mission to the North from Bremen. His biography by his successor Rimbert is an important source for 9th-century Scandinavia.
gruendung-von-dublin#summary: Norwegian Vikings set up a fortified ship camp at the mouth of the Liffey, from which the city of Dublin develops.
gruendung-von-dublin#text: The Irish annals record a fortified Viking winter camp, a so-called longphort, near Dublin in 841. From here the Northmen raided the interior, but they also traded, especially in slaves captured in Ireland. In the 10th century the camp grew into a trading town with workshops and a harbour, whose remains were uncovered by excavations at Wood Quay. Dublin remained a Scandinavian-ruled town until it was conquered by Anglo-Norman knights in 1170.
ende-des-bilderstreits#summary: Empress Theodora finally restores the veneration of images, an event the Orthodox Church still celebrates.
ende-des-bilderstreits#text: After the death of the iconoclast emperor Theophilos in 842, his widow Theodora ruled for their young son Michael III. In March 843 she had the decisions of 787 renewed, installed a pro-image patriarch and had the icons solemnly returned to the Hagia Sophia. The Orthodox Church commemorates this on the first Sunday of Lent, the Sunday of Orthodoxy. Since then icons have been an integral part of worship and devotion, and Byzantine art experienced a new flowering.
wikinger-pluendern-paris#summary: A Viking fleet sails up the Seine, sacks Paris at Easter 845 and withdraws only after being paid 7,000 pounds of silver.
wikinger-pluendern-paris#text: In the spring of 845 a fleet of some 120 ships sailed up the Seine; its leader is called Reginherus in the sources, whom some identify with the legendary Ragnar Lodbrok, though this is uncertain. On Easter Sunday the Vikings reached Paris and plundered the city. The West Frankish king Charles the Bald bought their departure with 7,000 pounds of silver, the first of many such payments in the Frankish realm. Because rivers allowed the ships to strike deep inland, cities such as Paris, Rouen and Nantes were attacked again and again in the following decades.
ostroute-nach-byzanz-und-bagdad#title: The Varangians on the Eastern Route
ostroute-nach-byzanz-und-bagdad#summary: Scandinavian traders and warriors, known in the East as Varangians or Rus, travel the rivers of eastern Europe as far as the Black Sea and the Caspian.
ostroute-nach-byzanz-und-bagdad#text: Already in the 8th century trading places such as Staraya Ladoga arose on Lake Ladoga, from which Scandinavians, mostly from present-day Sweden, travelled south along the Volga and the Dnieper. They traded furs and slaves for Arab silver and Byzantine goods; in 860 the Rus attacked Constantinople for the first time. In 922 the Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan described Rus traders and a ship burial on the Volga. Kievan Rus emerged from the rule of Varangian princes over East Slavic lands; later Scandinavians served in the Byzantine emperor’s Varangian Guard.
rjurik-und-die-berufung-der-waraeger#tit: Rurik and the Invitation of the Varangians
rjurik-und-die-berufung-der-waraeger#sum: According to the Primary Chronicle, the tribes around Novgorod invite the Varangian Rurik to rule them; the story is regarded as the founding legend of the Rus.
rjurik-und-die-berufung-der-waraeger#tex: The Primary Chronicle, compiled by monks in Kyiv in the early 12th century, reports that in 862, after internal strife, Slavic and Finnic tribes asked the Varangian Rurik and his brothers to become their princes. How much of this is historical cannot be said with certainty; the date was assigned in retrospect. Archaeological finds in Staraya Ladoga and Novgorod do show, however, that Scandinavian traders and warriors settled along the rivers of Eastern Europe in the 9th century and mixed with the Slavic population. How large their share in state formation was has been disputed since the 18th century. The Rurikid dynasty, which ruled in Moscow until 1598 and provided one more tsar in Vasily Shuisky (1606–1610), took its name from Rurik.
mission-von-kyrill-und-method#title: Cyril and Methodius Evangelize the Slavs
mission-von-kyrill-und-method#summary: Two brothers from Thessaloniki set out for Great Moravia, create a Slavic script and celebrate the liturgy in the Slavic language.
mission-von-kyrill-und-method#text: Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia asked Emperor Michael III for teachers who could preach Christianity in the language of his people. Constantine, later called Cyril, and his brother Methodius knew the Slavic language from their home region around Thessaloniki. Cyril developed the Glagolitic script and, with Methodius, translated biblical and liturgical texts. In Moravia they met resistance from Frankish clergy, but their disciples continued the work in Bulgaria, where the Cyrillic script emerged. In this way the Slavic church language became the foundation of the culture of many Eastern European peoples.
taufe-boris-von-bulgarien#title: Boris I of Bulgaria Is Baptized
taufe-boris-von-bulgarien#summary: The Bulgarian ruler adopts Christianity from Byzantium and leads his realm into the Orthodox world.
taufe-boris-von-bulgarien#text: Around 864 or 865 Khan Boris was baptized and took the name Michael after his godfather, Emperor Michael III. At first he wavered between Rome and Constantinople before the Bulgarian church was placed under the church of Constantinople in 870. From 886 Boris took in disciples of Cyril and Methodius, who founded Slavic schools in Ohrid and Preslav. Bulgaria thus became a centre of Slavic literary culture, while remaining a powerful rival of Byzantium in the Balkans.
grosses-heidnisches-heer#title: The Great Heathen Army Lands in England
grosses-heidnisches-heer#summary: A large Viking army lands in East Anglia and within a few years conquers the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and much of Mercia.
grosses-heidnisches-heer#text: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls the force that came ashore in East Anglia in 865 the “great army”; later tradition places Ivar and Halfdan, said to be sons of Ragnar Lodbrok, at its head. In 866 the Vikings took York, and in 869 they killed King Edmund of East Anglia, who was afterwards venerated as a saint. Unlike earlier raiding bands they stayed in the country for years, installed dependent kings and from 876 shared out land among their warriors. Only Wessex under Alfred the Great held out and defeated the army at Edington in 878.
makedonische-dynastie#summary: Basil I murders his co-emperor and founds a dynasty under which the empire flourishes for almost two centuries.
makedonische-dynastie#text: Basil I, a peasant's son from the region of Adrianople, had risen as a favourite of Michael III and had him murdered in 867. His dynasty ruled until 1056 and is named after his origins in the theme of Macedonia. In this period laws were renewed, Crete, Cyprus and Antioch were recovered and Bulgaria was subjugated. At the same time art, scholarship and court ceremonial flourished in what is called the Macedonian Renaissance.
besiedlung-islands#summary: According to tradition, Ingólfr Arnarson becomes the first permanent settler in Iceland in 874; within 60 years the island is settled.
besiedlung-islands#text: The Icelandic Book of Settlements (Landnámabók) names Ingólfr Arnarson as the first settler, who made his home around 874 on the site of present-day Reykjavík; older traces suggest that Irish monks had visited the island before. By about 930 thousands of settlers had arrived, mainly from western Norway, together with people from the Scandinavian settlements in the British Isles, among them many unfree Irish and Scots. They brought livestock and lived from pastoral farming and fishing. The clearing of the birch woods soon led to soil erosion that still marks the land today.
schlacht-bei-edington#title: Alfred’s Victory at Edington and the Danelaw
schlacht-bei-edington#summary: Alfred the Great defeats the Viking army under Guthrum at Edington; England is divided into an Anglo-Saxon and a Scandinavian-ruled area.
schlacht-bei-edington#text: Early in 878 Guthrum’s army took the king of Wessex by surprise, and he had to withdraw into the marshes of Athelney. In May Alfred gathered a new army and defeated the Vikings at Edington. Guthrum accepted baptism and moved with his people to East Anglia, where he ruled as king. In a later treaty the two fixed a boundary; the area to the north and east of it, where Scandinavian law applied, later came to be called the Danelaw. Place names ending in -by and -thorpe and many loanwords in English still recall this settlement.
oleg-macht-kiew-zur-hauptstadt#summary: The Varangian prince Oleg travels down the Dnieper from Novgorod, conquers Kyiv and joins the north and south of the Rus.
oleg-macht-kiew-zur-hauptstadt#text: According to the chronicle, Oleg ruled after Rurik's death on behalf of his young son Igor. Around 882 he sailed down the Dnieper, had the rulers of Kyiv, Askold and Dir, killed and declared Kyiv the "mother of the cities of the Rus". From there he subjugated neighbouring tribes, who had to pay him tribute in furs, honey and wax. A treaty with Byzantium of 911, whose text the chronicle preserves, regulated the trade of Rus merchants in Constantinople. In this way a centre of power arose on the trade route between the Baltic and the Black Sea that shaped the following centuries.
gruendung-des-klosters-cluny#summary: Duke William of Aquitaine founds the abbey of Cluny in Burgundy and places it directly under the protection of the pope; it becomes the starting point of a great monastic reform.
gruendung-des-klosters-cluny#text: In the foundation charter of 910 William the Pious renounced all influence and made the abbey subject to the pope alone, so that neither bishops nor lay lords could control it. Under energetic abbots such as Odo, Odilo and Hugh the reform spread, demanding strict observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict, solemn liturgy and independence from laymen. Hundreds of monasteries across Europe joined Cluny. The movement strengthened the papacy and prepared the ground for the church reform of the 11th century; the third abbey church of Cluny was the largest church in Christendom until the new St Peter’s was built.
vertrag-von-saint-clair-sur-epte#summary: The West Frankish king Charles the Simple cedes the land around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo; from it the Duchy of Normandy emerges.
vertrag-von-saint-clair-sur-epte#text: After a failed attack on Chartres, Rollo reached an agreement with Charles the Simple at Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, according to tradition in 911: he received the territory on the lower Seine, was to be baptized and was to defend the land against other Vikings. No text of the treaty survives; the detailed account comes from the chronicler Dudo of Saint-Quentin, writing about a hundred years later. Rollo’s successors extended the territory, adopted the language and religion of the Franks and as dukes of Normandy became one of the strongest powers in France. Their descendant William conquered England in 1066.
gruendung-des-althing#summary: The free men of Iceland gather for the first time at Þingvellir for the Althing, which makes laws and decides disputes.
gruendung-des-althing#text: According to tradition the Althing first met around 930 on the plain of Þingvellir in southwestern Iceland. It sat for two weeks every summer; the goðar, chieftains with priestly and political roles, formed the law-making assembly, and an elected lawspeaker recited the law in force from memory. There were also courts in which disputes and killings were tried. An executive power was lacking, however: the parties had to enforce judgements themselves. The Althing is regarded as one of the oldest popular assemblies in Europe; Þingvellir is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
schlacht-am-bach-dang-938#title: Battle of the Bạch Đằng River
schlacht-am-bach-dang-938#summary: Ngô Quyền destroys a fleet of the Southern Han dynasty and ends roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule over what is now northern Vietnam.
